claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Expression of Per1 but not Per2 mRNA was induced in synchronized NIH 3T3 fibroblast cells after forskolin treatment.
claims.source: In accordance with our in vivo experiments (Figure 6), expression of Per1 but not Per2 mRNA was induced in synchronized NIH 3T3 fibroblast cells after forskolin treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d and e, blue bars).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d and e.

claims.claim: Per1 induction by forskolin was abolished in Cdk5 ko cells.
claims.source: Comparable to the experiments in the SCN, Per1 induction was abolished in Cdk5 ko cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: Fos mRNA induction was not affected in Cdk5 ko cells.
claims.source: In contrast, Fos mRNA induction was not affected in Cdk5 ko cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1f), consistent with our observations in the SCN (Figure 6g).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1f.

claims.claim: Cdk5 regulates light- and forskolin-mediated expression of genes critical for the regulation of phase delays of the circadian clock.
claims.source: Collectively, our expression data provide evidence that Cdk5 regulates light- and forskolin-mediated expression of genes critical for the regulation of phase delays of the circadian clock.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined gene expression data from in vivo and in vitro experiments.

claims.claim: The phenotype of Cdk5 knock-down in the SCN of mice resembled the phenotypes observed in Per2 mutant and neuronal Per2 knock-out mice.
claims.source: The phenotype of Cdk5 knock-down (shCdk5) in the SCN of mice resembled the phenotypes observed in Per2 mutant (Per2Brdm1) and neuronal Per2 knock-out (nPer2 ko) mice.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the behavioral phenotypes across different mouse models.

claims.claim: Cdk5 is involved in the regulation of the circadian clock mechanism via nuclear localization of PER2.
claims.source: Our results indicate that Cdk5 is not only involved in the regulation of the circadian clock mechanism via nuclear localization of PER2 but also plays an important role in the molecular mechanism that leads to a delay of clock phase in response to a light pulse in the early dark phase or early subjective night.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge from previous studies by the authors.

claims.claim: Cdk5 plays an important role in the molecular mechanism that leads to a delay of clock phase in response to a light pulse in the early dark phase or early subjective night.
claims.source: Our results indicate that Cdk5 is not only involved in the regulation of the circadian clock mechanism via nuclear localization of PER2 but also plays an important role in the molecular mechanism that leads to a delay of clock phase in response to a light pulse in the early dark phase or early subjective night.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined behavioral and molecular data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CaMKII but not of MAPK affected light-induced phase delays in hamsters.
claims.source: Pharmacological inhibition of CaMKII but not of MAPK affected light-induced phase delays in hamsters (Yokota et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Darpp-32 ko mice show attenuated phase delays.
claims.source: Furthermore, Darpp-32 ko mice show attenuated phase delays (Yan et al., 2006) resembling shCdk5 mice (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Lack of Per1, Dec1, Sik1, Gem, Fos, or Egr1 alone does not abolish phase delays.
claims.source: Interestingly, neither lack of Per1, Dec1(Albrecht et al., 2001; Rossner et al., 2008) nor Sik1 or Gem (Jagannath et al., 2013; Matsuo et al., 2022) alone abolish phase delays. Of note is that lack of Fos or Egr1 did not affect phase delays either (Honrado et al., 1996; Riedel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: VIP is important in circadian light responses.
claims.source: Furthermore, the neuropeptide VIP, which is important in circadian light responses (Jones et al., 2018), was not inducible by a light pulse at ZT14 in control as well as shCdk5 animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), indicating that Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling.
claims.source: Furthermore, the neuropeptide VIP, which is important in circadian light responses (Jones et al., 2018), was not inducible by a light pulse at ZT14 in control as well as shCdk5 animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), indicating that Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of Cdk5 knockdown on VIP expression.

claims.claim: Cdk5 not only regulates the light-sensitive PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway but ultimately also affects gene expression.
claims.source: Overall, the present data suggest that Cdk5 not only regulates the light-sensitive PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway but ultimately also affects gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined signaling and gene expression data.

claims.claim: Nuclear PER2 protein is necessary for transcriptional activation of light-responsive genes.
claims.source: For the transcriptional activation of those genes, nuclear PER2 protein is necessary, which is regulated by Cdk5 (Brenna et al., 2021; Brenna et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The combination of lack of induction of many genes in the Cdk5-regulated pathway is responsible for the manifestation of rapid behavioral phase delays.
claims.source: The combination of lack of induction of many genes in the Cdk5-regulated pathway is responsible for the manifestation of rapid behavioral phase delays.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined effects of Cdk5 on multiple genes and the behavioral phenotype.

claims.claim: Cdk5 is active right after dark onset.
claims.source: As reported previously, Cdk5 is active right after dark onset (Brenna et al., 2019), depicted as the active Cdk5/p35 complex (blue).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Active Cdk5 phosphorylates PER2, which translocates to the nucleus.
claims.source: This has two consequences: (1) PER2 (red) is phosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus (Brenna et al., 2019), and (2) DARPP32 is phosphorylated and thus inhibits PKA activity (Bibb et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Phosphorylated DARPP32 inhibits PKA activity.
claims.source: This has two consequences: (1) PER2 (red) is phosphorylated and translocates to the nucleus (Brenna et al., 2019), and (2) DARPP32 is phosphorylated and thus inhibits PKA activity (Bibb et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Before the light pulse at ZT14, the nucleus is supplied with PER2, which appears to be necessary for light-mediated behavioral phase delays.
claims.source: Hence, before the light pulse at ZT14, the nucleus is supplied with PER2, which appears to be necessary for light-mediated behavioral phase delays (Albrecht et al., 2001; Spoelstra et al., 2004; Chavan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Light at ZT14 evokes glutamate and PACAP release at the synapses between the RHT and the SCN.
claims.source: This state can then be dramatically changed when light is applied at ZT14 (Figure 7b) evoking glutamate and PACAP release at the synapses between the RHT and the SCN.
claims.evidence: This represents established knowledge about neurotransmitter release in response to light.

claims.claim: Light at ZT14 abolishes the interaction between p35 and Cdk5, thereby inactivating Cdk5.
claims.source: Interaction between p35 and Cdk5 is abolished (Figure 2) thereby inactivating Cdk5 and stopping phosphorylation of PER2 and DARPP32.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: PKA phosphorylates Cav3.1.
claims.source: At the same time, PKA becomes phosphorylated due to PACAP and cAMP signaling, leading to activation of Cav3.1 by PKA (Figure 5f; Kim et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Phospho-CREB builds up a complex with CRTC1/CBP and PER2 to activate gene expression.
claims.source: Phospho-CREB builds up a complex with CRTC1/CBP and PER2 (Brenna et al., 2021) to activate gene expression of the Per1, Dec1, Sik1, and Gem genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The amount of PER2 protein in the nucleus may determine at least in part the magnitude of the phase delay.
claims.source: In the activation complex the amount of PER2 present in the nucleus may at least in part affect the magnitude of the phase delay, which is depending on the time the light pulse is given.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the role of PER2 in the transcriptional complex and the timing-dependent effects of light.

claims.claim: Cdk5 activity gates both the pre-light condition and the post-light condition.
claims.source: In conclusion, Cdk5 activity is gating both processes, the pre-light condition and the post-light condition, leading to a concerted activation of a set of light-responsive genes that impinge on behavioral phase delays in response to nocturnal light exposure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing Cdk5's role in regulating both PER2 nuclear localization and the light signaling pathway.

results.result: Cdk5 knockdown in the SCN specifically impairs light-induced phase delays at ZT14/CT14 but not phase advances at ZT22/CT22, and shortens the circadian period under constant darkness. This phenotype was observed in both male and female mice using both Aschoff type I and II protocols.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C49-C60 provide converging behavioral evidence from wheel-running activity experiments showing that Cdk5 knockdown selectively abolishes phase delays while preserving phase advances. The data are consistent across multiple time points (ZT14, CT14 vs ZT22, CT22), both sexes, and different experimental protocols, with appropriate controls and statistical significance reported.

results.result: Light at ZT14 increases p35 protein levels but decreases Cdk5 kinase activity by disrupting the Cdk5/p35 complex formation. Despite increased p35 levels, less p35 co-immunoprecipitates with Cdk5 after light exposure, indicating light-mediated dissociation of the active complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C68 are supported by western blot, kinase activity assays, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2). The paradoxical finding that p35 increases while Cdk5 activity decreases is explained by reduced complex formation, demonstrated by co-IP data. The mechanism of light-induced dissociation remains unclear but the observations are internally consistent.

results.result: Cdk5 gates light-induced phosphorylation of CREB, CaMKII, and CaMKIV in the SCN. In shCdk5 animals, these kinases are constitutively phosphorylated even in the absence of light, indicating that Cdk5 normally suppresses their activation until a light signal is received.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C79 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 3a, b, d) showing that phosphorylation of CREB-S133, CaMKII, and CaMKIV is light-dependent in controls but constitutive in shCdk5 animals. This demonstrates Cdk5's gating function, though the molecular mechanism of suppression is not fully elucidated. Quantification and statistical analysis support the conclusions.

results.result: Cdk5 regulates the subcellular localization of calmodulin (CAM) and the T-type calcium channel Cav3.1. Light induces perinuclear CAM localization and membrane localization of Cav3.1 in control animals, but these localization patterns are constitutive in shCdk5 animals independent of light.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 3c, e) showing altered localization patterns of CAM and Cav3.1. The data demonstrate that Cdk5 regulates protein trafficking/localization, consistent with cited literature on Cdk5's role in channel and receptor translocation. Quantification supports the observations.

results.result: Light-induced calcium influx in SCN neurons is significantly dampened in shCdk5 animals compared to controls, as measured by in vivo fiber photometry using GCaMP7 calcium indicators.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by fiber photometry data (Figure 4b, c) showing reduced calcium responses during and after light pulses in shCdk5 mice. The use of in vivo calcium imaging provides direct evidence for Cdk5's role in regulating calcium dynamics. Statistical analysis confirms significant differences, though the mechanism linking Cdk5 to calcium influx requires further investigation.

results.result: Cdk5 is required for sustained CREB phosphorylation in response to forskolin stimulation, as demonstrated by FRET experiments showing that Cdk5 ko cells fail to maintain CREB phosphorylation. This effect is calcium-dependent, as calcium depletion or chelation abolishes the response.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 and C96 are supported by FRET data (Figure 5a, b) showing differential CREB phosphorylation dynamics in control vs Cdk5 ko cells. The calcium dependence experiments strengthen the conclusion that Cdk5 modulates CREB phosphorylation via calcium signaling. However, the FRET approach measures phosphorylation indirectly, and the first 5 minutes are excluded due to DMSO artifacts, which could affect interpretation.

results.result: CREB is phosphorylated by CaMKIV rather than directly by PKA, as demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation showing that p-CaMKIV but not p-PKA interacts with CREB in SCN tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b, c) showing differential interaction of CREB with p-CaMKIV versus p-PKA. This challenges previous models suggesting direct PKA-CREB interaction and is consistent with the nuclear localization of CaMKIV versus cytoplasmic PKA. However, the negative result (no PKA-CREB interaction) should be interpreted cautiously as it could reflect technical limitations.

results.result: Cdk5 regulates PKA activity via DARPP32 phosphorylation. Light reduces DARPP32 phosphorylation at Thr-75 in control animals, releasing PKA from inhibition. In shCdk5 animals, DARPP32 phosphorylation is constitutively low and PKA is constitutively active, independent of light.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 5d, e) showing inverse correlation between DARPP32 and PKA phosphorylation states. The data are consistent with the established DARPP32-PKA regulatory pathway and explain how Cdk5 gates PKA activity. Statistical analysis supports the conclusions, though the mechanism by which light reduces DARPP32 phosphorylation is not fully explained.

results.result: Cdk5 gates the interaction between phospho-PKA and Cav3.1 in response to light. Co-localization of p-PKA and Cav3.1 increases dramatically after light in control animals but is constitutively high in shCdk5 animals, suggesting Cdk5 regulates PKA-mediated activation of calcium channels via DARPP32.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are supported by co-localization immunohistochemistry data (Figure 5f) showing light-dependent PKA-Cav3.1 interaction in controls versus constitutive interaction in shCdk5 animals. This provides a mechanistic link between Cdk5, PKA, and calcium channel regulation. However, co-localization does not prove direct interaction, and functional validation of PKA-mediated Cav3.1 activation would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Light induces Per1 and Dec1 but not Per2, Dec2, or Bmal1 mRNA expression in the SCN at ZT14. Cdk5 knockdown abolishes light-induced Per1 and Dec1 expression while not affecting the non-light-responsive genes, demonstrating Cdk5's specific role in light-induced clock gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C119 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 6a-e) showing selective effects of Cdk5 knockdown on light-inducible genes. The differential effects on Per1/Dec1 versus Per2/Dec2/Bmal1 demonstrate specificity. Statistical analysis supports the conclusions, and the results are consistent with previous literature on light-induced gene expression patterns.

results.result: Cdk5 knockdown differentially affects immediate early gene expression: Fos induction by light is preserved while Egr1 induction is abolished, suggesting that Fos and Egr1 are regulated by distinct mechanisms in response to light at ZT14.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C122 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 6g, h) showing differential effects of Cdk5 knockdown on Fos versus Egr1. This demonstrates that not all light-induced genes require Cdk5, suggesting multiple parallel pathways. The inference that Fos uses a different mechanism is reasonable but the alternative pathway is not characterized.

results.result: Cdk5 regulates light-induced expression of negative regulators Sik1 and Gem, which limit the magnitude of phase shifts. Knockdown of Cdk5 abolishes light-induced expression of both genes, suggesting Cdk5 coordinates both the activation and limitation of light responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 and C130-C132 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 6i, j) showing abolished light induction of Sik1 and Gem in shCdk5 animals. This reveals that Cdk5 regulates both positive and negative components of the light response pathway. The observation that Gem may be slightly elevated at baseline in shCdk5 animals (C132) requires further investigation but doesn't undermine the main conclusion.

results.result: In vitro forskolin treatment of synchronized NIH 3T3 cells recapitulates the in vivo findings: Per1 but not Per2 is induced by forskolin in control cells, and this induction is abolished in Cdk5 ko cells. Fos induction is preserved in Cdk5 ko cells, consistent with in vivo observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 are supported by qPCR data from cell culture experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d-f). The in vitro system validates the in vivo findings and demonstrates that Cdk5's role in gene regulation is cell-autonomous. The parallel between forskolin and light responses supports the use of forskolin as a surrogate for light signaling in cell culture.

results.result: Cdk5 serves as a master regulator that gates both pre-light and post-light conditions: before light, Cdk5 ensures PER2 nuclear accumulation while suppressing the PKA-CaMK-CREB pathway; after light, Cdk5 inactivation allows coordinated activation of light-responsive genes. The combination of effects on multiple genes is responsible for behavioral phase delays.
results.evaluation: Claims C138, C140, C146, C148, and C158 represent integrative conclusions supported by the combined behavioral, molecular, and imaging data throughout the manuscript. The model that Cdk5 gates both arms of the light response (PER2 availability and signaling pathway activation) is well-supported. However, some mechanistic details remain unclear, such as how light disrupts the Cdk5-p35 interaction.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on circadian clock biology, including the role of the SCN, light signaling pathways, phase response curves, and the differential roles of Per1 and Per2 in phase advances versus delays. This establishes the context for investigating Cdk5's role.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C12-C35 represent established knowledge from the circadian biology field, supported by appropriate citations. These background claims provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study. They are accurately presented and properly attributed to prior work.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior knowledge about voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), their classification into T-type and L-type channels, their differential roles in phase delays versus advances, and Cdk5's known functions including regulation of T-type channels and PER2 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C48 represent established knowledge about calcium channels and Cdk5, supported by appropriate citations including the authors' previous work. This background is essential for understanding the rationale for investigating Cdk5 in light-induced phase shifts. The information is accurately presented.

results.result: The manuscript cites extensive prior literature on light-induced signaling pathways, including the roles of CRE elements, CREB phosphorylation, PKA signaling, DARPP32, and various regulatory genes (Sik1, Gem). This establishes the known framework within which Cdk5's role is being investigated.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72, C90-C91, C95, C100, C111-C112, C125, C129, C133, C141-C144, C147, C149-C153, C155-C156 represent prior knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These claims establish the mechanistic framework and are essential for interpreting the new findings about Cdk5. The citations appear accurate and relevant.

results.result: The manuscript cites prior work showing that Cdk5 plays important roles in channel and receptor translocation, and that circadian calcium fluxes in SCN neurons have been demonstrated in vitro and respond rapidly to light.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 represent prior knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide context for interpreting the observed effects of Cdk5 on Cav3.1 localization and calcium dynamics. The citations are relevant and support the statements made.

results.result: VIP expression in the SCN is not induced by light at ZT14 in either control or shCdk5 animals, indicating that Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling rather than regulating VIP expression itself.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 and C145 are supported by qPCR data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a) showing no light induction of Vip. The inference that Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling (C145) is reasonable given that VIP is important for light responses but its expression is not Cdk5-dependent. However, this is a negative result and alternative interpretations exist.

results.result: The amount of PER2 protein in the nucleus may determine at least in part the magnitude of the phase delay, depending on the timing of the light pulse.
results.evaluation: Claim C157 is explicitly labeled as speculation in the evidence field. While the model proposes that nuclear PER2 levels affect phase delay magnitude, this is not directly tested in the manuscript. The claim is plausible based on the data showing PER2's role in the transcriptional complex, but lacks direct experimental support for the dose-response relationship proposed.

results.result: Cdk5 activity is modulated by light and specifically regulates phase delays but not phase advances of the circadian clock. Knockdown of Cdk5 in the SCN impairs light-induced phase delays at ZT14/CT14 while leaving phase advances at ZT22/CT22 intact.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. The editor states the study 'suggests that light modulated activity of Cdk5 activity...provides missing molecular mechanistic details to understand light-induced circadian clock phase delays during the early night, but not for phase advances.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors have convincingly demonstrated that Cdk5 plays a critical role in gating the light-induced phase-shifting response' and Reviewer 2 confirms 'first evidence for the specific involvement of CdK5 in light-induced phase advance [delay] of the free-running rhythm.'

results.result: Light increases p35 protein levels but decreases Cdk5 kinase activity by disrupting the Cdk5/p35 complex formation. Co-immunoprecipitation shows reduced p35 binding to Cdk5 after light exposure at ZT14.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these molecular findings. Reviewer 1 states the data is 'well-presented in clear figures and appropriately described in the text' and that 'the set of experiments performed in this work is non-trivial, done to a high standard.' The editor acknowledges the study provides 'convincing evidence bridging from behavioral to molecular/cellular experiments,' implicitly accepting these mechanistic details.

results.result: Cdk5 knockdown leads to constitutive, light-independent activation of the PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway. In shCdk5 animals, CREB, CaMKII, and CaMKIV are phosphorylated even before light exposure, and Cav3.1 channels are localized to the membrane independently of light.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states the study 'suggests that light modulated activity of Cdk5 activity on the PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway provides missing molecular mechanistic details.' Reviewer 2 confirms the study reveals Cdk5's 'mode of action through PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway.' No reviewer challenges the immunohistochemistry or signaling data showing constitutive pathway activation in Cdk5 knockdown conditions.

results.result: Calcium fluxes in the SCN increase during and after light pulses in control mice, but this response is significantly dampened in Cdk5 knockdown animals, as measured by fiber photometry.
results.evaluation: The editor notes the authors provide 'convincing evidence bridging from behavioral to molecular/cellular experiments to neural activity imaging,' explicitly acknowledging the calcium imaging data. Reviewer 2 highlights 'experimental approaches are carried from in-vivo, to cellular and molecular level,' supporting acceptance of the fiber photometry findings.

results.result: Cdk5 knockdown abolishes light-induced expression of Per1, Dec1, Egr1, Sik1, and Gem genes, while Fos induction remains intact. This demonstrates Cdk5's role in regulating specific light-responsive gene expression critical for phase delays.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the gene expression data. Reviewer 1 states 'the data is well-presented in clear figures and appropriately described in the text' and affirms the authors' conclusions are 'strongly support[ed]' by their results. The differential effect on Fos versus other genes is not challenged, supporting the claim that Cdk5 regulates specific subsets of light-responsive genes.

results.result: Cdk5 gates PKA activity via DARPP32 phosphorylation. Light reduces DARPP32 phosphorylation in controls, but Cdk5 knockdown causes constitutively low DARPP32 phosphorylation and elevated PKA activity. This leads to increased PKA-Cav3.1 co-localization even before light exposure in shCdk5 animals.
results.evaluation: The editor's statement that the study provides 'missing molecular mechanistic details' for the PKA-CaMK-CREB pathway implicitly accepts the DARPP32-PKA mechanism. Reviewer 1 notes the experiments are 'done to a high standard' and the conclusions are 'strongly support[ed].' No reviewer challenges the DARPP32 phosphorylation data or the proposed gating mechanism.

results.result: FRET experiments in cultured cells show that Cdk5 is involved in CREB phosphorylation dynamics. Cdk5 knockout cells show altered CREB phosphorylation kinetics in response to forskolin, and calcium chelation experiments support that CREB phosphorylation is modulated by Cdk5 via calcium signaling.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises 'the set of experiments performed in this work is non-trivial, done to a high standard' and notes the authors employed 'a combination of molecular, cellular, and behavioural techniques.' The FRET data is not challenged by any reviewer, and the overall mechanistic model is accepted.

results.result: Immunoprecipitation experiments suggest that CREB is phosphorylated by CaMKIV rather than directly by PKA, with PKA likely regulating CaMKIV indirectly. CREB did not co-immunoprecipitate with phospho-PKA but did interact with phospho-CaMKIV.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this mechanistic detail. Reviewer 1 states the data is 'well-presented' and 'appropriately described,' and no concerns are raised about the immunoprecipitation experiments or the proposed indirect PKA-CaMKIV-CREB pathway.

results.result: Silencing Cdk5 in the SCN reduces Cdk5 and PER2 expression and shortens the circadian period in constant darkness. The period shortening is not influenced by light pulses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes the study provides 'first evidence for the specific involvement of CdK5' in circadian regulation, implicitly accepting the period phenotype. The behavioral data showing period shortening is part of the overall accepted experimental framework.

results.result: Light increases phosphorylation of PKA, CaMKII, and CREB in the SCN at ZT14, as measured by Western blot.
results.evaluation: These are confirmatory experiments ensuring proper light induction. Reviewer 1 notes the experiments are 'done to a high standard' and reviewers do not question these basic validation experiments. The editor's acceptance of the overall PKA-CaMK-CREB mechanism implicitly supports these foundational observations.

results.result: Fos expression is induced by light independently of Cdk5, suggesting it is regulated by a different mechanism than Egr1, Per1, and Dec1. This is observed both in vivo in the SCN and in vitro in Cdk5 knockout cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this differential gene regulation finding. Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'there could be additional mechanisms which the authors have duly acknowledged and discussed in their text,' supporting the interpretation that Fos uses an alternative pathway. The data is accepted as part of the comprehensive gene expression analysis.

results.result: VIP expression is not induced by light at ZT14 in either control or shCdk5 animals, suggesting Cdk5 acts upstream of VIP signaling and does not regulate phase shifts via VIP.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question this negative result. The finding helps define the boundaries of Cdk5's mechanism and is accepted as part of the overall experimental framework without challenge.

results.result: In synchronized NIH 3T3 fibroblast cells, forskolin induces Per1 but not Per2 expression, and this Per1 induction is abolished in Cdk5 knockout cells, recapitulating the in vivo findings.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the authors employed 'a combination of molecular, cellular, and behavioural techniques' and that experiments are 'done to a high standard.' The in vitro validation of in vivo findings is not challenged and supports the robustness of the conclusions.

results.result: The overall model proposes that Cdk5 gates both pre-light and post-light conditions: before light, Cdk5 phosphorylates PER2 for nuclear localization (necessary for phase delays), and after light, Cdk5 inactivation releases the brake on PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling. The combination of effects on multiple genes is responsible for behavioral phase delays.
results.evaluation: The editor states the study 'provides missing molecular mechanistic details' and all reviewers accept the overall model. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors have convincingly demonstrated that Cdk5 plays a critical role in gating the light-induced phase-shifting response' and that their 'results strongly support their conclusions.' Reviewer 2 is 'happy with the manuscript in its present form,' indicating acceptance of the integrated model.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the core behavioral finding that Cdk5 knockdown selectively abolishes phase delays while preserving phase advances. OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence across multiple time points and protocols (C5-C7, C49-C60), while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as the study's central contribution with quotes from all reviewers confirming the convincing demonstration of Cdk5's gating role.

Both support the molecular findings on Cdk5-p35 complex dynamics (C64-C68). OpenEval notes the paradoxical p35 increase with decreased Cdk5 activity is explained by reduced complex formation, though the mechanism remains unclear. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the high-standard molecular work without challenge, acknowledging the study provides missing mechanistic details.

Both support the immunohistochemistry data showing constitutive phosphorylation of CREB-S133, CaMKII, and CaMKIV in shCdk5 animals (C73-C79). OpenEval also includes protein localization findings (C80-C83). Peer reviewers explicitly accept the PKA-CaMK-CREB signaling pathway mechanism as providing missing molecular details, with no challenges to the immunohistochemistry data.

Perfect agreement on calcium imaging data (C88-C89). OpenEval supports the fiber photometry findings showing reduced calcium responses in shCdk5 mice, noting the mechanism requires further investigation. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge the neural activity imaging as convincing evidence bridging behavioral to molecular experiments.

Both support the FRET data on CREB phosphorylation dynamics (C92-C94, C96). OpenEval notes the indirect measurement and DMSO artifact exclusion as potential limitations. Peer reviewers praise the non-trivial, high-standard experiments and accept the overall mechanistic model without challenging the FRET approach.

Both support the immunoprecipitation data showing differential CREB interaction with p-CaMKIV versus p-PKA (C97-C99). OpenEval cautions about interpreting negative results (no PKA-CREB interaction) due to potential technical limitations. Peer reviewers accept this mechanistic detail as well-presented and appropriately described without raising concerns.

Both support the DARPP32-PKA regulatory mechanism (C101-C106). OpenEval notes statistical support but incomplete explanation of how light reduces DARPP32 phosphorylation. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the missing mechanistic details for the PKA-CaMK-CREB pathway, with experiments done to high standard.

Both support PKA-Cav3.1 interaction data (C108-C110). OpenEval notes co-localization doesn't prove direct interaction and suggests functional validation would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall gating mechanism without specific concerns about the co-localization approach.

Both support the qPCR data on light-inducible genes (C113-C119). OpenEval emphasizes selective effects and differential regulation of Per1/Dec1 versus Per2/Dec2/Bmal1. Peer reviewers accept the gene expression data as well-presented with strongly supported conclusions, part of the comprehensive experimental framework.
